Credit Card Fraud Detection Using Machine Learning¶

Domain: Finance / Banking / Fraud Analytics  |  End consumer: Fraud Risk Manager / Fraud Analytics Team ML problem: Imbalanced binary classification  |  Target: Class (0 = legitimate, 1 = fraudulent)

Every number, table, chart and insight in this notebook is computed from the uploaded creditcard.csv file. Narrative answers were written only after the code was executed and refer to the printed outputs directly above them.

Contents

  1. Business Understanding · 2. Environment & Libraries · 3. Data Loading · 4. Data Exploration · 5. Data Quality Assessment · 6. Data Cleaning & Preparation · 7. 10 Business KPIs · 8. 10 Univariate Analyses · 9. 10 Bivariate Analyses · 10. 10 Multivariate Analyses · 11. Feature Engineering & Preprocessing · 12. Train/Validation/Test Strategy · 13. Baseline Model · 14. Imbalance Handling · 15. Model Building & Comparison · 16. Evaluation, Threshold Analysis & Explainability · 17. Final Business Report

Stage 1 — Business Understanding¶

Business problem. A card issuer processes a very large number of transactions, a tiny share of which are fraudulent. Every fraudulent transaction that goes undetected is a direct financial loss (plus chargeback handling cost and reputational damage), while every legitimate transaction that is wrongly flagged creates friction: a declined purchase, a call to the customer, or analyst time spent on a false alarm.

Project objective. Analyse the transaction data to understand how fraudulent transactions differ from legitimate ones, and build a model that assigns each transaction a fraud-risk score so that the riskiest transactions can be blocked, challenged or reviewed, while keeping the number of unnecessary alerts on legitimate customers manageable.

Stakeholder / end consumer. The Fraud Risk Manager and Fraud Analytics Team, who own the alerting strategy, the review queue and the fraud-loss budget.

Why fraud detection matters. Fraud losses are direct, they erode customer trust, and card schemes and regulators expect issuers to monitor transactions effectively.

Error type What it means Business consequence
False negative (fraud predicted as legitimate) A fraudulent transaction is approved Direct monetary loss, chargeback cost, customer harm
False positive (legitimate predicted as fraud) A genuine customer is declined or challenged Customer friction, lost interchange revenue, analyst workload, potential churn

Why class imbalance matters. Fraud is extremely rare in this dataset (quantified in Stage 3). A model that labels every transaction as legitimate would therefore look more than 99.8% "accurate" while catching zero fraud. Accuracy is consequently not used to judge models; instead the project uses precision, recall, F1, PR-AUC (Average Precision), ROC-AUC and the confusion matrix, with particular emphasis on fraud recall and precision-recall performance.

Success criteria.

  1. All findings are reproducible and computed from the data.
  2. No data leakage: the test set is held out until the very end and never resampled.
  3. The selected model clearly beats a naive baseline on PR-AUC and fraud recall on the untouched test set.
  4. The precision/recall trade-off is made explicit through threshold analysis so the Fraud Risk Manager can choose an operating point.

Problem statement. Using 48 hours of anonymised card transactions, develop and evaluate a leakage-free machine-learning model that ranks transactions by fraud risk, maximising the share of fraud detected (recall) while keeping the precision of alerts at a level that a review team can act on.

Dataset structure (from the outputs above). The file contains 284,807 rows and 31 columns, all numeric: Time (float, seconds elapsed since the first transaction), V1–V28 (float, anonymised principal components), Amount (float, transaction amount) and the target Class (int64, values 0 and 1 only). There are no missing values and 1,081 exact duplicate rows. Fraud makes up 492 rows (0.1727%) before cleaning. Each row is a single transaction; there is no cardholder, merchant, or terminal identifier, so transactions cannot be linked to customers.

What each variable represents.

  • Time – seconds elapsed between each transaction and the first transaction in the file. It runs from 0 to 172,792 s, i.e. 48 hours (2 days). It is not a clock time or date.
  • V1–V28 – outputs of a principal component analysis carried out by the data provider on undisclosed original features. Consistent with that, every component has mean ≈ 0 (largest |mean| 4.9e-15) and the standard deviations decrease monotonically from V1 (1.96) to V28 (0.33), exactly the ordering PCA produces. Their original business meaning is unknown and is not guessed at in this project.
  • Amount – transaction amount (currency not stated). Median 22.00, mean 88.35, maximum 25,691.16.
  • Class – 1 for fraud, 0 for legitimate.

First class comparison. Fraud has a lower median amount than legitimate transactions (9.25 vs 22.00 in the raw data) but a higher mean (122.21 vs 88.29) and a higher 75th percentile (105.89 vs 77.05), which hints that fraud is concentrated at both very small and fairly large amounts. Fraud's median Time is also earlier (75,569 s vs 84,711 s). Both points are examined properly in Stages 8–9.

Stage 5 — Data Quality Assessment¶

In [9]:
num = df_raw.select_dtypes("number")
dup_mask = df_raw.duplicated(keep="first")
n_dup = int(dup_mask.sum())
n_dup_fraud = int(df_raw.loc[dup_mask, TARGET].sum())

# Same feature values but different labels would indicate label noise
conflicts = df_raw.groupby(FEATURES)[TARGET].nunique()
n_conflict_groups = int((conflicts > 1).sum())

n_inf = int(np.isinf(num).sum().sum())
n_missing = int(df_raw.isna().sum().sum())
n_neg_amount = int((df_raw.Amount < 0).sum())
n_zero_amount = int((df_raw.Amount == 0).sum())
n_zero_amount_fraud = int(((df_raw.Amount == 0) & (df_raw[TARGET] == 1)).sum())
q1, q3 = df_raw.Amount.quantile([0.25, 0.75])
amount_upper_fence = q3 + 1.5 * (q3 - q1)
n_amount_outliers = int((df_raw.Amount > amount_upper_fence).sum())
time_monotonic = bool(df_raw.Time.is_monotonic_increasing)
n_time_neg = int((df_raw.Time < 0).sum())
labels_ok = set(df_raw[TARGET].unique()) == {0, 1}
int_like_time = bool((df_raw.Time % 1 == 0).all())

dq_summary = pd.DataFrame([
    ["Missing values", f"{n_missing} missing cells in any column", n_missing, "None required"],
    ["Exact duplicate rows", f"{n_dup} duplicate rows ({n_dup_fraud} labelled fraud)", n_dup,
     "Remove (keep first) to avoid identical rows in train and test"],
    ["Conflicting labels", f"{n_conflict_groups} identical feature vectors with different labels", n_conflict_groups,
     "None required" if n_conflict_groups == 0 else "Investigate"],

     "Keep: plausible card-verification / auth checks; potentially informative"],

     n_amount_outliers, "Keep: extreme values may carry fraud signal; use log transform + scaling"],

In [10]:
# Potential outliers in every numeric predictor (1.5 x IQR rule) - informational only
def iqr_outlier_count(s):
    q1, q3 = s.quantile([0.25, 0.75]); iqr = q3 - q1
    return int(((s < q1 - 1.5 * iqr) | (s > q3 + 1.5 * iqr)).sum())

outlier_table = pd.DataFrame({
    "outliers": {c: iqr_outlier_count(df_raw[c]) for c in FEATURES},
}).assign(pct=lambda d: 100 * d.outliers / len(df_raw))
outlier_table["fraud_rate_among_outliers_%"] = [
    100 * df_raw.loc[(df_raw[c] < df_raw[c].quantile(.25) - 1.5*(df_raw[c].quantile(.75)-df_raw[c].quantile(.25))) |
                     (df_raw[c] > df_raw[c].quantile(.75) + 1.5*(df_raw[c].quantile(.75)-df_raw[c].quantile(.25))), TARGET].mean()
    for c in FEATURES]
display(outlier_table.sort_values("pct", ascending=False).head(10))
print(f"Overall fraud rate for comparison: {100*df_raw[TARGET].mean():.3f}%")

Data quality summary. The dataset is technically clean: no missing values, no infinite values, no negative amounts, only the labels 0/1, correct numeric types, and Time sorted ascending in whole seconds. Three items need attention:

  1. 1,081 exact duplicate rows (19 of them fraud) – removed in Stage 6 (none have conflicting labels).
  2. Outliers are widespread but informative. Amount has 31,904 rows above the IQR fence (184.51). More importantly, rows that are outliers on components such as V14 (3.04% fraud rate), V12 (2.66%) or V21 (1.68%) have fraud rates 10–18 times the overall 0.173%. Removing outliers would remove fraud, so they are kept.
  3. 1,825 zero-amount transactions (27 fraud) are kept as plausible, not erroneous.

Stage 6 — Data Cleaning & Preparation¶

In [11]:
# 1) Remove exact duplicate rows (the only cleaning step justified by Stage 5)
df = df_raw.drop_duplicates(keep="first").reset_index(drop=True)
print(f"Rows before: {len(df_raw):,} | after: {len(df):,} | removed: {len(df_raw) - len(df):,}")
print(f"Fraud before: {df_raw[TARGET].sum()} | after: {df[TARGET].sum()} | "
      f"fraud rate after: {100*df[TARGET].mean():.4f}%")

# 2) Outliers, zero amounts and extreme PCA values are deliberately KEPT.

# 3) Analysis-only helper columns (used for EDA, NOT fed to the models)
eda = df.copy()
eda["Hour"] = ((eda["Time"] // 3600) % 24).astype(int)         # elapsed hour within each 24h window (not clock time)
eda["Day"] = (eda["Time"] // 86400).astype(int) + 1
eda["LogAmount"] = np.log1p(eda["Amount"])
AMOUNT_BINS = [-0.01, 0, 1, 10, 50, 100, 250, 500, 1000, np.inf]
AMOUNT_LABELS = ["0", "0-1", "1-10", "10-50", "50-100", "100-250", "250-500", "500-1000", ">1000"]
eda["AmountBand"] = pd.cut(eda["Amount"], bins=AMOUNT_BINS, labels=AMOUNT_LABELS)
print(eda[["Hour", "Day", "LogAmount", "AmountBand"]].head())

Cleaning decisions and leakage safeguards

Change Reason
Removed exact duplicate rows (keep first) Identical rows could land in both training and test sets, which would inflate test scores (a form of leakage). No conflicting labels were found, so nothing is lost informationally.
Kept all outliers (Amount and V1–V28) Stage 5 showed that outlying values in several PCA components carry a fraud rate far above the base rate; deleting them would delete fraud signal.
Kept zero-amount transactions Plausible (e.g. card checks) and not an error; they are a small group whose fraud behaviour is analysed below.
No imputation There are no missing values.
Hour, Day, LogAmount, AmountBand Created in a separate eda copy for descriptive analysis only. Model inputs come from df, and all fitted transformations (log/scaling) happen inside pipelines fitted on training data only.

Exploratory analysis in Stages 7–10 is descriptive and uses the full cleaned dataset; no modelling choice (feature selection, thresholds, hyperparameters) is fitted on it. Every fitted step from Stage 11 onwards is learned from the training split only.

KPI interpretation (cleaned data: 283,726 transactions)

# KPI Result Interpretation Why the Fraud Risk Manager should care
1 Total Transactions 283,726 Two days of card activity after de-duplication Sets the scale of the monitoring problem and of any alert-rate target
2 Fraudulent Transactions 473 Fewer than 500 confirmed frauds Very few examples to learn from, so every metric on fraud is statistically noisy
3 Legitimate Transactions 283,253 The vast majority of customers are genuine Every false alert lands on one of these customers
4 Fraud Rate 0.1667% About 1 fraud in every 600 transactions Explains why accuracy is meaningless: "approve everything" is 99.83% accurate
5 Total Transaction Value 25,102,001.68 Total value processed in two days Denominator for loss-rate reporting
6 Fraudulent Transaction Value 58,591.39 Gross fraud exposure over the window The loss the model is trying to prevent
7 Legitimate Transaction Value 25,043,410.29 Genuine spend Value put at risk of friction by false declines
8 Average Fraud Amount 123.87 Larger on average than genuine transactions… …so each missed fraud costs more than an average transaction
9 Average Legitimate Amount 88.41 Typical genuine spend Benchmark for amount-based rules
10 Fraud Value % of Total 0.2334% Fraud's share of value is 1.40× its share of count Measured in money, fraud matters more than counts suggest

The supporting cell shows that the median fraud amount (9.82) is less than half the median legitimate amount (22.00), even though the mean is 1.40× higher. Fraud amounts are therefore polarised: many very small fraudulent transactions plus a tail of large ones. A single "average amount" KPI hides this, which matters for any amount-based rule.

U1. Class — how rare is fraud?¶

Business question: How rare is fraud in our transaction stream, and what does this imply for alert volumes?

Technical question: What is the frequency distribution of the binary target, and what is the imbalance ratio?

In [15]:
counts = df[TARGET].value_counts().sort_index()
imbalance_ratio = counts[0] / counts[1]
print(counts.rename(CLASS_NAMES).to_string())
print(f"Fraud share: {100*counts[1]/counts.sum():.4f}% | Imbalance ratio: 1 fraud per {imbalance_ratio:,.0f} legitimate")
print(f"Accuracy of 'always legitimate': {100*counts[0]/counts.sum():.3f}%")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
ax.bar([CLASS_NAMES[i] for i in counts.index], counts.values, color=[CLASS_COLORS[i] for i in counts.index])
for i, v in enumerate(counts.values):
    ax.text(i, v * 1.15, f"{v:,}", ha="center")
ax.set_yscale("log"); ax.set_title("U1. Class distribution (log scale)"); ax.set_ylabel("Transactions")
save_fig("u1_class")

Class
Legitimate    283253
Fraud            473
Fraud share: 0.1667% | Imbalance ratio: 1 fraud per 599 legitimate
Accuracy of 'always legitimate': 99.833%

Answer (business): Fraud is extremely rare: 473 frauds versus 283,253 legitimate transactions (0.1667%), or about 1 fraud per 599 genuine transactions.

Answer (technical): The target is severely imbalanced (ratio ≈ 1:599). A constant 'legitimate' prediction already scores 99.833% accuracy.

Insight: Any model must be judged on fraud-focused metrics (recall, precision, PR-AUC). Splits must be stratified so validation and test sets each contain enough fraud to evaluate.

U2. Amount — raw distribution¶

Business question: What does a typical transaction amount look like, and are there very large transactions?

Technical question: What are the central tendency, spread, skewness and kurtosis of Amount?

In [16]:

pct = a.quantile([.01, .05, .25, .5, .75, .95, .99, .999])
print(pct.rename(lambda q: f"P{q*100:g}").round(2).to_string())
print(f"Mean {a.mean():.2f} | Median {a.median():.2f} | Std {a.std():.2f} | Max {a.max():,.2f}")
print(f"Skewness {a.skew():.2f} | Excess kurtosis {a.kurt():.2f}")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4))
axes[0].hist(a, bins=100, color="#4C72B0"); axes[0].set_title("U2a. Amount (full range)"); axes[0].set_yscale("log")
axes[1].hist(a[a <= a.quantile(.99)], bins=80, color="#4C72B0"); axes[1].set_title("U2b. Amount up to the 99th percentile")
for ax in axes: ax.set_xlabel("Amount")
save_fig("u2_amount")

P1          0.1200
P5          0.9200
P25         5.6000
P50        22.0000
P75        77.5100
P95       365.3400
P99     1,018.9600
P99.9   3,004.7500
Mean 88.47 | Median 22.00 | Std 250.40 | Max 25,691.16
Skewness 16.98 | Excess kurtosis 844.47

Answer (business): A typical transaction is small: half are 22.00 or less and three quarters are 77.51 or less. A small number are very large; the largest is 25,691.16, against a 99th percentile of 1,018.96.

Answer (technical): Amount is extremely right-skewed (skewness 16.98, excess kurtosis 844.47). The mean (88.47) is four times the median (22.00).

Insight: Raw Amount is dominated by a long tail. Distance-based or linear models would be pulled around by a few huge values, which motivates a log transform (U3). Medians and percentiles describe this variable better than the mean.

U3. Amount — log transformation¶

Business question: Can we represent transaction size in a way that stops a few very large purchases from dominating the model?

Technical question: Does a log(1 + Amount) transformation materially reduce skewness?

In [17]:
la = np.log1p(df["Amount"])
print(f"Skewness raw Amount   : {df['Amount'].skew():.2f}")
print(f"Skewness log1p(Amount): {la.skew():.2f}")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4))
ax.hist(la, bins=80, color="#55A868"); ax.set_xlabel("log(1 + Amount)")
ax.set_title("U3. Distribution of log-transformed Amount")
save_fig("u3_log_amount")

Skewness raw Amount   : 16.98
Skewness log1p(Amount): 0.16

Answer (business): Yes. On a log scale, transaction sizes spread out evenly, so very large purchases no longer dominate.

Answer (technical): Skewness drops from 16.98 to 0.16 after log(1 + Amount), which is close to symmetric. The log-scale histogram is spiky, with tall bars at specific values that are consistent with frequently repeated amounts.

Insight: log1p(Amount) is adopted in the preprocessing pipeline (Stage 11). It is applied inside the pipeline, so it involves no fitted parameters; the scaling step after it is fitted on training data only.

U4. Amount — outliers¶

Business question: How many unusually large transactions are there, and how much value do they represent?

Technical question: How many observations exceed the 1.5×IQR upper fence of Amount, and what share of total value do they hold?

In [18]:
q1, q3 = df.Amount.quantile([.25, .75]); fence = q3 + 1.5 * (q3 - q1)
out = df.Amount > fence
print(f"IQR upper fence: {fence:.2f}")
print(f"Outlying transactions: {out.sum():,} ({100*out.mean():.2f}% of count)")
print(f"Share of total value held by outliers: {100*df.loc[out,'Amount'].sum()/df.Amount.sum():.2f}%")
print(f"Fraud rate among outliers: {100*df.loc[out,TARGET].mean():.3f}% vs {100*df.loc[~out,TARGET].mean():.3f}% for the rest")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 2.8))
ax.boxplot(df.Amount, vert=False, flierprops=dict(marker=".", alpha=.2, markersize=3))
ax.set_xscale("symlog"); ax.set_xlabel("Amount (symlog scale)"); ax.set_title("U4. Amount box plot")
save_fig("u4_amount_box")

IQR upper fence: 185.38
Outlying transactions: 31,685 (11.17% of count)
Share of total value held by outliers: 64.74%
Fraud rate among outliers: 0.275% vs 0.153% for the rest

Answer (business): 31,685 transactions (11.17%) are unusually large by the IQR rule (above 185.38), and they account for 64.74% of all transaction value. Their fraud rate is 0.275%, compared with 0.153% for the rest.

Answer (technical): The 1.5×IQR upper fence of Amount is 185.38; 11.17% of observations exceed it, which is far more than a symmetric distribution would produce.

Insight: These 'outliers' are a normal, large segment of the business that carries most of the value and a higher fraud rate. They must not be deleted.

U6. Time — distribution over the observation window¶

Business question: How is transaction activity spread over the observation period?

Technical question: What is the shape of the Time distribution (elapsed seconds), and is it uniform?

Answer (business): Activity is not uniform. Both days show the same daily cycle, with a deep trough and a long busy plateau. The two days have similar volume (144,236 vs 139,490).

Answer (technical): The Time distribution is bimodal. The busiest elapsed hour (hour 21 of the window) has 9,875 transactions and the quietest (hour 4) only 1,082, a factor of about 9.

Insight: The repeating pattern is consistent with a day/night cycle, but because Time starts at an unknown clock time, the troughs cannot be labelled as 'night' with certainty.

Answer (business): Yes. Elapsed hours 1–6 together carry only 7.15% of transaction volume, whereas hours 9–22 each carry roughly 15,000–17,600 transactions.

Answer (technical): The 24-bucket distribution (Time // 3600 mod 24) is strongly non-uniform, with a trough at hours 1–6 (minimum at hour 4: 2,204).

Insight: Quiet periods are a natural place to examine fraud rates (B4). In periods of low genuine activity, a fixed number of frauds forms a larger share of traffic.

Technical question: What are the skewness and excess kurtosis of each of the 30 predictors?

Answer (business): Extreme values are concentrated in a few components: V27 (13.67% of rows beyond the IQR fences), V28 (10.61%), V20 (9.71%), V8 (8.43%) and V6 (8.07%). The median component has 3.20%, and the minimum is 0.26%.

Answer (technical): IQR outlier prevalence varies by a factor of about 50 across components, so heavy tails are a feature of specific components rather than random noise.

Insight: Outlier prevalence and fraud relevance are different things. Many of the most outlier-heavy components (V27, V28, V20) are not the top fraud separators (V14, V10, V12, V4). Blanket outlier removal would therefore be both unjustified and harmful.

Stage 9 — 10 Bivariate Analyses¶

Each analysis relates one predictor to Class (or two predictors to each other). Statistical tests describe association only; association does not imply causation. With hundreds of thousands of rows, even tiny differences become "significant", so effect sizes (KS statistic, differences in medians, fraud-rate ratios) are emphasised over p-values.

In [25]:
def fraud_rate_table(group_col, data=eda):
    """Count, fraud count and fraud rate (%) per group, with lift vs the overall rate."""
    g = data.groupby(group_col, observed=True)[TARGET].agg(transactions="size", frauds="sum")
    g["fraud_rate_%"] = 100 * g["frauds"] / g["transactions"]
    g["lift_vs_overall"] = g["fraud_rate_%"] / (100 * data[TARGET].mean())
    return g

def class_hist(feature, ax, bins=60, data=df, log=False):
    """Overlay density histograms of a feature for each class."""
    lo, hi = data[feature].quantile([.0005, .9995])
    for k in (0, 1):
        vals = data.loc[data[TARGET] == k, feature].clip(lo, hi)
        ax.hist(vals, bins=bins, density=True, alpha=.55, color=CLASS_COLORS[k], label=CLASS_NAMES[k])
    ax.set_title(feature); ax.legend()
    if log: ax.set_yscale("log")

B1. Class vs Amount¶

Business question: Are fraudulent transactions larger or smaller than genuine ones?

Technical question: Do the distributions of Amount differ between classes (Mann–Whitney U test, medians, quantiles)?

In [26]:
q = df.groupby(TARGET)["Amount"].quantile([.25, .5, .75, .9, .99]).unstack().rename(index=CLASS_NAMES)
display(q.round(2))
mw = stats.mannwhitneyu(fraud.Amount, legit.Amount, alternative="two-sided")
print(f"Mann-Whitney U p-value: {mw.pvalue:.3e}")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
ax.boxplot([np.log1p(legit.Amount), np.log1p(fraud.Amount)], showfliers=False); ax.set_xticks([1, 2], ["Legitimate", "Fraud"])
ax.set_ylabel("log(1 + Amount)"); ax.set_title("B1. Amount by class (log scale, outliers hidden)")
save_fig("b1_amount_class")
0.2500 0.5000 0.7500 0.9000 0.9900
Class
Legitimate 5.6700 22.0000 77.4600 203.0000 1,018.0600
Fraud 1.0000 9.8200 105.8900 348.6500 1,364.1400 
Mann-Whitney U p-value: 2.686e-05

Answer (business): Fraud is both smaller and larger. A quarter of frauds are 1.00 or less (legitimate: 5.67), and the fraud median is 9.82 versus 22.00. Above the median the pattern flips: the fraud 75th, 90th and 99th percentiles (105.89, 348.65, 1,364.14) exceed the legitimate ones (77.46, 203.00, 1,018.06).

Answer (technical): The Mann–Whitney U test rejects equal distributions (p = 2.7e-05). The difference is a change in shape (more mass in both tails) rather than a simple shift.

Insight: Amount alone is a weak, two-sided signal. Small 'test' transactions and larger transactions both deserve attention, which a single 'amount > X' rule cannot capture. This is a statistical association, not evidence of fraudster intent.

B2. Fraud rate by Amount band¶

Business question: Which transaction-size bands carry the highest fraud risk?

Technical question: Is fraud rate independent of amount band (chi-square test of independence)?

Answer (business): Zero-amount transactions are the riskiest band (1.38% fraud, 8.3× the overall rate), followed by 0–1 (0.51%, 3.1×) and 500–1,000 (0.40%, 2.4×). Mid-range 10–50 transactions are the safest (0.061%, 0.37×).

Answer (technical): Fraud rate depends on amount band (χ² = 481.1, 8 df, p ≈ 8e-99).

Insight: The risk curve is U-shaped. Micro and zero-value transactions plus high-value transactions are where amount-based scrutiny adds most. Note that the >1,000 band contains only 9 frauds, so its rate is imprecise.

B3. Class vs Time¶

Business question: Does fraud follow the same timing pattern as normal activity?

Technical question: Are the Time distributions of the two classes different (two-sample KS test)?

In [28]:
ks = stats.ks_2samp(fraud.Time, legit.Time)
print(f"KS statistic = {ks.statistic:.3f}, p = {ks.pvalue:.3e}")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 4))
for k in (0, 1):
    ax.hist(df.loc[df[TARGET] == k, "Time"] / 3600, bins=48, density=True, alpha=.55,
            color=CLASS_COLORS[k], label=CLASS_NAMES[k])
ax.set_xlabel("Elapsed hours"); ax.set_ylabel("Density"); ax.legend()
ax.set_title("B3. Time distribution by class (normalised within class)")
save_fig("b3_time_class")

KS statistic = 0.160, p = 4.468e-11

Answer (business): No. Fraud does not follow the daily cycle of genuine activity. It does not drop much in the quiet periods and shows sharp spikes (for example around elapsed hours 2–3, 11 and 26–28) that genuine traffic does not have.

Answer (technical): The two-sample KS test finds a difference (KS = 0.160, p ≈ 4.5e-11). This is a modest effect compared with the leading PCA components (KS up to 0.84).

Insight: Because fraud does not follow the daily cycle, its rate should rise in low-traffic periods (B4). The spikes are consistent with frauds arriving in bursts, but with two days of data and no card identifiers this is a hypothesis, not a finding.

B4. Fraud rate by elapsed hour¶

Business question: Are some hours of the day riskier, even if fraud volume is lower?

Technical question: How does the fraud rate vary across elapsed-hour buckets, and is the variation significant?

Insight: Low-traffic periods are disproportionately risky. Caveat: with only two days of data, each hour bucket holds just two observations of that hour, and 'hour' is relative to an unknown start time, so this pattern should be confirmed on a longer history before building rules on it.

B5. Linear association of every predictor with Class¶

Business question: Which variables move most consistently with fraud?

Technical question: What is the point-biserial correlation between each predictor and Class?

Answer (business): V17 (r = −0.313), V14 (−0.293), V12 (−0.251), V10 (−0.207) and V16 (−0.187) have the strongest negative association with fraud. V11 (0.149) and V4 (0.129) have the strongest positive association.

Answer (technical): Point-biserial correlations are all |r| ≤ 0.31. With a 0.17% prevalence, the maximum attainable correlation is strongly capped, so these are respectable values.

Insight: Correlation identifies a consistent shortlist of components but understates separation for rare classes and captures linear association only, which motivates the KS view in B6. Correlation is not causation, and these components have no known business meaning.

B6. Distributional separation (KS) of every predictor¶

Business question: Beyond linear correlation, which variables look most different between fraud and genuine transactions?

Technical question: How large is the two-sample KS statistic for each predictor, and how does that ranking compare with correlation?

Answer (technical): The KS ranking (top: V14 = 0.838) broadly agrees with correlation but re-orders it. V4 and V11 rank 4th–5th by KS while ranking lower by |r|, because their fraud distributions are shifted and spread out, which correlation captures less well.

Insight: The anonymised components, not Amount or Time, carry most of the separable signal. This is why the six top-KS components are used for the profiling below.

axes[0].scatter(s.Time / 3600, s.Amount, s=3, alpha=.3); axes[0].set_yscale("symlog")
axes[0].set_xlabel("Elapsed hours"); axes[0].set_ylabel("Amount"); axes[0].set_title("B10a. Amount vs Time (20k sample)")
axes[1].bar(hr_med.index, hr_med.values, color="#55A868"); axes[1].set_xlabel("Elapsed hour")
axes[1].set_title("B10b. Median amount by elapsed hour")
save_fig("b10_amount_time")

Spearman rho(Time, Amount) = -0.040 (p = 8.65e-100)
Median amount by elapsed hour ranges from 11.85 (hour 5) to 33.00 (hour 10)

Answer (business): Only slightly. Median amount varies by elapsed hour from 11.85 (hour 5) to 33.00 (hour 10), so transactions in the quiet hours tend to be smaller.

Answer (technical): Spearman ρ(Time, Amount) = −0.040. The association is statistically significant only because of the very large sample size and is negligible in practice.

Insight: Time and Amount are nearly independent, so each brings separate (if modest) information. The smaller amounts in quiet hours also matter for M5, where low amount and quiet hours combine.

Stage 10 — 10 Multivariate Analyses¶

M1. Overall correlation structure¶

Business question: Do our variables carry overlapping (redundant) information?

Technical question: What does the full Pearson correlation matrix of all 31 columns look like, given that V1–V28 are PCA outputs?

In [36]:
corr = df.corr()
off = corr.loc[V_COLS, V_COLS].where(~np.eye(len(V_COLS), dtype=bool)).abs()
print(f"Max |corr| between two different V components: {off.max().max():.4f}")
amt_corr = corr["Amount"].drop(["Amount", TARGET]).sort_values(key=abs, ascending=False)
time_corr = corr["Time"].drop(["Time", TARGET]).sort_values(key=abs, ascending=False)
print("Strongest correlations with Amount:"); print(amt_corr.head(5).round(3).to_string())
print("Strongest correlations with Time:"); print(time_corr.head(3).round(3).to_string())
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 8.5))
im = ax.imshow(corr, cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-1, vmax=1)
ax.set_xticks(range(len(corr))); ax.set_xticklabels(corr.columns, rotation=90, fontsize=8)
ax.set_yticks(range(len(corr))); ax.set_yticklabels(corr.columns, fontsize=8)
ax.grid(False); plt.colorbar(im, fraction=.046); ax.set_title("M1. Correlation matrix (all transactions)")
save_fig("m1_corr")

Answer (business): Not among the PCA components: they are essentially uncorrelated (the largest |r| between two different components is 0.019). Amount and Time, however, are correlated with some components (Amount with V2: −0.533, V7: 0.400, V5: −0.388, V20: 0.341; Time with V3: −0.422).

Answer (technical): This is what PCA predicts: components are orthogonal by construction. Amount and Time were left outside the PCA, but the original features evidently related to them, so they partially overlap with some components.

Insight: Multicollinearity among V1–V28 is not a concern. Amount is partly redundant with V2/V7/V5, so it should not be over-interpreted in feature-importance results.

M2. Correlation structure within the fraud class¶

Business question: Do fraudulent transactions show a distinctive, coordinated pattern across variables?

Technical question: How do pairwise correlations among the top-separating components differ between fraud-only and legitimate-only data?

In [37]:
cols = TOP_V
c_f = fraud[cols].corr(); c_l = legit[cols].corr()
mask = ~np.eye(len(cols), dtype=bool)
print(f"Mean |corr| among {cols}: fraud = {c_f.where(mask).abs().stack().mean():.3f} | legitimate = {c_l.where(mask).abs().stack().mean():.3f}")
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5))
for ax, c, t in zip(axes, [c_l, c_f], ["Legitimate only", "Fraud only"]):
    im = ax.imshow(c, cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-1, vmax=1); ax.grid(False)
    ax.set_xticks(range(len(cols))); ax.set_xticklabels(cols); ax.set_yticks(range(len(cols))); ax.set_yticklabels(cols)
    for i in range(len(cols)):
        for j in range(len(cols)):
            ax.text(j, i, f"{c.iloc[i, j]:.2f}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8)
    ax.set_title(f"M2. {t}")
save_fig("m2_corr_within_class")

Mean |corr| among ['V14', 'V10', 'V12', 'V4', 'V11', 'V17']: fraud = 0.742 | legitimate = 0.088

Answer (business): Yes. Within fraud, the top components move together strongly (mean |r| = 0.742 among V14, V10, V12, V4, V11, V17), whereas among legitimate transactions they are nearly unrelated (mean |r| = 0.088).

Answer (technical): Correlation structure is class-dependent. The PCA orthogonality holds over the whole dataset (dominated by legitimate rows) but breaks down inside the fraud subset.

Insight: Fraud has a coordinated multivariate signature: when one top component is extreme, the others usually are too. This supports multivariate models over single-variable rules and explains why tree ensembles can separate fraud well.

M3. Top two components jointly with Class¶

Business question: Would combining the two strongest signals separate fraud better than either alone?

Technical question: How do fraud and legitimate transactions sit in the 2-D space of the top two KS components?

In [38]:
f1, f2 = TOP_V[0], TOP_V[1]
s0 = legit.sample(15000, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 6))
ax.scatter(s0[f1], s0[f2], s=4, alpha=.25, c=CLASS_COLORS[0], label="Legitimate (15k sample)")
ax.scatter(fraud[f1], fraud[f2], s=10, alpha=.7, c=CLASS_COLORS[1], label="Fraud (all)")
ax.set_xlabel(f1); ax.set_ylabel(f2); ax.legend(); ax.set_title(f"M3. {f1} vs {f2} by class")
save_fig("m3_scatter_top2")
# Share of each class in the joint lower tail (both below legit 1st percentile)
t1, t2 = legit[f1].quantile(.01), legit[f2].quantile(.01)
for name, d in [("Fraud", fraud), ("Legitimate", legit)]:
    print(f"{name}: {100*((d[f1] < t1) | (d[f2] < t2)).mean():.1f}% below legit P1 on {f1} OR {f2}; "
          f"{100*((d[f1] < t1) & (d[f2] < t2)).mean():.2f}% below on both")

Fraud: 85.2% below legit P1 on V14 OR V10; 77.59% below on both
Legitimate: 1.9% below legit P1 on V14 OR V10; 0.07% below on both

Answer (business): Combining helps mainly by confirming signals. 85.2% of frauds fall below the legitimate 1st percentile on V14 or V10, against only 1.9% of legitimate transactions. Requiring both still keeps 77.6% of fraud while cutting legitimate transactions to 0.07%.

Answer (technical): In the V14–V10 plane, fraud forms an elongated cloud extending down-left from the dense legitimate cluster near the origin, with some overlap where a minority of frauds sit close to the legitimate centre.

Insight: Joint conditions trade a small loss in recall for a large reduction in false positives. This is the same precision/recall trade-off formalised later by the model threshold. Some frauds lie inside the legitimate cluster and will be hard for any model to detect.

M4. Pairwise view of four strong components¶

Business question: Is the fraud pattern consistent across several variables at once?

Technical question: Do pairwise scatter plots of four top-ranked components show fraud consistently occupying a distinct region?

In [39]:

samp = pd.concat([legit.sample(5000, random_state=RANDOM_STATE), fraud])

Answer (business): Yes. In every pair among V14, V10, V12 and V4, fraud (red) occupies a consistent region away from the compact legitimate cluster: low on V14/V10/V12 and high on V4.

Answer (technical): The pair plot shows fraud spread along a roughly linear direction in each plane, which is consistent with the strong within-fraud correlations found in M2.

Insight: The fraud pattern is consistent across several variables at once, which is favourable for multivariate classifiers. A residual group of frauds overlaps the legitimate cluster in every panel.

M5. Amount + Time + Class¶

Business question: Is there a combination of transaction size and time of day where fraud concentrates?

Technical question: How does fraud rate vary jointly across elapsed hour (grouped into 6-hour blocks) and amount band?

M6. High-value transactions + top component + Class¶

Business question: Among high-value transactions, can a PCA signal isolate the risky ones?

Technical question: Within the top 5% of Amount, how does fraud rate differ between transactions in the fraud-like tail of the top component and the rest?

In [41]:

M8. Count of extreme signals as a simple multivariate risk indicator¶

Business question: If several variables are simultaneously unusual, how much riskier is the transaction?

Technical question: Counting how many of the top-6 components fall in their fraud-like tail (beyond the legitimate P1/P99), how does fraud rate change with the count?

In [43]:
def tail_flags(data):
    """1 if a component is beyond the legitimate-class P1 (negative shift) or P99 (positive shift)."""
    flags = pd.DataFrame(index=data.index)
    for c in TOP_V:
        d = np.sign(fraud[c].median() - legit[c].median())
        flags[c] = (data[c] < legit[c].quantile(.01)) if d < 0 else (data[c] > legit[c].quantile(.99))
    return flags.astype(int)

eda["ExtremeCount"] = tail_flags(eda).sum(axis=1)
ec = fraud_rate_table("ExtremeCount")
ec["share_of_all_fraud_%"] = 100 * ec.frauds / ec.frauds.sum()
display(ec)
print(f"Fraud captured with >=2 extreme signals: {ec.loc[ec.index >= 2, 'frauds'].sum()} of {len(fraud)} "
      f"while flagging {ec.loc[ec.index >= 2, 'transactions'].sum():,} transactions")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4))
ax.bar(ec.index.astype(str), ec["fraud_rate_%"], color=CLASS_COLORS[1]); ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xlabel(f"Number of top components in fraud-like tail ({', '.join(TOP_V)})"); ax.set_ylabel("Fraud rate % (log)")
ax.set_title("M8. Fraud rate vs number of simultaneous extreme signals")
save_fig("m8_extreme_count")

Answer (business): Risk rises steeply with the number of simultaneous extreme signals: 0.022% fraud with none, 1.34% with two, 11.3% with three, and 64–88% with four or more. Requiring at least two signals captures 398 of 473 frauds (84.1%) while flagging 1,913 transactions (0.67% of traffic).

Answer (technical): A simple count of how many of the top-6 components lie beyond the legitimate P1/P99 shows a near-monotonic dose–response relationship with fraud rate.

Insight: Even a transparent, hand-built score separates fraud strongly. However, 59 frauds (12.5%) show no extreme signal and would be missed by such rules, so they form a structurally hard segment. This multivariate profile is used for understanding only; it is not a model input, so it introduces no leakage.

Answer (business): No, Amount is linked to some PCA components, and the link is weaker for fraud. The correlation of Amount with V2 is −0.538 among legitimate transactions but −0.270 among frauds. For V7 it is 0.417 vs 0.196, and for V5 −0.393 vs −0.063.

Answer (technical): The Amount–component relationships are class-dependent. In the scatter plots, frauds deviate from the band that legitimate transactions follow, and several frauds share identical amounts (visible as horizontal lines of red points near 1 and near 100) across very different component values.

Insight: For fraud, the usual relationship between amount and the underlying (anonymised) transaction characteristics breaks down. A model can exploit this inconsistency, and it is one reason interaction-capable models such as trees are expected to beat a purely linear model.

Stage 11 — Feature Engineering & Preprocessing¶

Design decisions (justified by Stages 4–10)

  • Amount → log(1 + Amount) → standardisation. U2/U3 showed Amount is extremely right-skewed and the log transform removes most of the skew. This mainly helps the linear model; tree models are invariant to monotonic transforms.
  • Time → standardisation. Time is elapsed seconds over only two days, so it cannot be converted into reliable calendar features (day of week, true clock hour). The Hour column used in EDA is a relative construct and is deliberately not added as a model feature, to avoid encoding an artefact of this particular two-day window.
  • V1–V28 → standardisation only. These are already PCA outputs (centred, near-uncorrelated – M1). They should not be reinterpreted as business attributes: each component is a linear mixture of unknown original variables, so "V14 is low" cannot be translated into a statement about, say, the merchant or the cardholder. They are used as numeric signals only.
  • No feature selection, no dropping of outliers. All 30 predictors go to every model.
  • Everything fitted lives inside a Pipeline. The scaler (and SMOTE where used) is fitted on training folds only, so validation and test data never influence preprocessing.
In [46]:
def make_preprocessor():
    """log1p + scale Amount, scale Time, scale V1-V28. Fitted only on whatever data the pipeline is fitted on."""
    amount_pipe = Pipeline([("log1p", FunctionTransformer(np.log1p, feature_names_out="one-to-one")),
                            ("scale", StandardScaler())])
    return ColumnTransformer([("amount", amount_pipe, ["Amount"]),
                              ("time", StandardScaler(), ["Time"]),
                              ("pca", StandardScaler(), V_COLS)],

List of (name, transformer, columns) tuples specifying the

Like in Pipeline and FeatureUnion, this allows the transformer and
its parameters to be set using ``set_params`` and searched in grid
search.
transformer : {'drop', 'passthrough'} or estimator
Estimator must support :term:`fit` and :term:`transform`.
Special-cased strings 'drop' and 'passthrough' are accepted as
well, to indicate to drop the columns or to pass them through
untransformed, respectively.
columns : str, array-like of str, int, array-like of int, array-like of bool, slice or callable
Indexes the data on its second axis. Integers are interpreted as
positional columns, while strings can reference DataFrame columns
by name. A scalar string or int should be used where
``transformer`` expects X to be a 1d array-like (vector),
otherwise a 2d array will be passed to the transformer.
A callable is passed the input data `X` and can return any of the
above. To select multiple columns by name or dtype, you can use
:obj:`make_column_selector`. 		[('amount', ...), ('time', ...), ...]
remainder remainder: {'drop', 'passthrough'} or estimator, default='drop'

By default, only the specified columns in `transformers` are
transformed and combined in the output, and the non-specified
columns are dropped. (default of ``'drop'``).
By specifying ``remainder='passthrough'``, all remaining columns that
were not specified in `transformers`, but present in the data passed
to `fit` will be automatically passed through. This subset of columns
is concatenated with the output of the transformers. For dataframes,
extra columns not seen during `fit` will be excluded from the output
of `transform`.
By setting ``remainder`` to be an estimator, the remaining
non-specified columns will use the ``remainder`` estimator. The
estimator must support :term:`fit` and :term:`transform`.
Note that using this feature requires that the DataFrame columns
input at :term:`fit` and :term:`transform` have identical order. 		'drop'

Stage 12 — Train / Validation / Test Strategy¶

  • Training set (60%) – used to fit preprocessing, resampling and models.
  • Validation set (20%) – used to compare models and to choose the decision threshold.
  • Test set (20%) – locked away and used once, at the end, to report final performance.

All splits are stratified on Class, so the rare fraud class is represented at the same rate in each split. The split happens before any scaling or resampling, so nothing learnt from validation/test data can leak into training.

In [47]:

y = df[TARGET]

No index overlap between splits.

Result. The stratified 60/20/20 split produced 170,235 / 56,745 / 56,746 rows containing 284 / 94 / 95 frauds, with fraud rates of 0.1668% / 0.1657% / 0.1674%, all matching the overall 0.1667%. No index overlaps. Note that with fewer than 100 frauds in validation and in test, each fraud moves recall by about one percentage point. This is why results are reported with counts and, for the test set, bootstrap intervals.

Why random rather than time-based splitting? With only 48 hours of data, a temporal split would leave one day for training and a few hours for testing, with very few frauds. A random stratified split is used here, and temporal validation is listed as a future improvement (the production model would always predict the future).

Stage 13 — Baseline Model¶

Two baselines are built:

  1. Naive "always legitimate" classifier (DummyClassifier) – shows why accuracy is misleading.
  2. Plain Logistic Regression – no imbalance handling; the simplest honest model to beat.

All models in Stages 13–15 are evaluated on the validation set; the test set stays untouched.

In [48]:
def evaluate(name, y_true, proba, threshold=0.5):
    """Return a dict of imbalance-aware metrics for one model at a given threshold."""
    pred = (proba >= threshold).astype(int)
    tn, fp, fn, tp = confusion_matrix(y_true, pred, labels=[0, 1]).ravel()
    return {"Model": name, "Threshold": threshold,
            "Precision": precision_score(y_true, pred, zero_division=0),
            "Recall": recall_score(y_true, pred, zero_division=0),
            "F1": f1_score(y_true, pred, zero_division=0),
            "ROC-AUC": roc_auc_score(y_true, proba),
            "PR-AUC": average_precision_score(y_true, proba),
            "Accuracy": accuracy_score(y_true, pred),
            "TP": tp, "FP": fp, "FN": fn, "TN": tn}

def fit_and_score(name, estimator, results, store):
    """Fit on training data, score on validation data, keep the fitted model and probabilities."""
    t0 = time.time()
    estimator.fit(X_train, y_train)
    proba = estimator.predict_proba(X_val)[:, 1]
    res = evaluate(name, y_val, proba); res["Fit_seconds"] = round(time.time() - t0, 1)
    results.append(res); store[name] = {"model": estimator, "val_proba": proba}
    return res

def plot_cm(y_true, pred, title, fname):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.5, 4))
    ConfusionMatrixDisplay(confusion_matrix(y_true, pred, labels=[0, 1]),
                           display_labels=["Legitimate", "Fraud"]).plot(ax=ax, cmap="Blues", values_format=",d", colorbar=False)
    ax.grid(False); ax.set_title(title)
    save_fig(fname)

RESULTS, MODELS = [], {}
fit_and_score("Naive: always legitimate", Pipeline([("prep", make_preprocessor()),
              ("clf", DummyClassifier(strategy="most_frequent"))]), RESULTS, MODELS)
fit_and_score("Baseline: Logistic Regression", Pipeline([("prep", make_preprocessor()),
              ("clf", LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000, random_state=RANDOM_STATE))]), RESULTS, MODELS)
baseline_tbl = pd.DataFrame(RESULTS).set_index("Model")
display(baseline_tbl.drop(columns=["Threshold", "Fit_seconds"]))
plot_cm(y_val, (MODELS["Baseline: Logistic Regression"]["val_proba"] >= .5).astype(int),
        "Baseline LR – validation", "s13_baseline_cm")

Results (validation set: 56,745 transactions, 94 frauds).

  • The naive "always legitimate" model scores 99.83% accuracy but catches 0 of 94 frauds (recall 0, PR-AUC 0.0017, equal to the fraud prevalence). This is the clearest demonstration that accuracy is useless here.
  • Plain Logistic Regression achieves precision 0.878, recall 0.691 (65 caught, 29 missed, 9 false alarms), F1 0.774, ROC-AUC 0.975 and PR-AUC 0.798. Its accuracy (99.93%) is barely different from the naive model's, yet its business value is completely different.

This logistic regression is the benchmark that more complex models must beat, chiefly on PR-AUC and fraud recall.

Stage 14 — Imbalance Handling¶

Strategy How it works Advantages Disadvantages
A. Class weighting Misclassifying a fraud costs more in the loss function (class_weight="balanced") No synthetic data, no extra rows, fast Usually raises recall at the cost of precision at the default threshold; weights are a blunt instrument
B. SMOTE (training only) Synthesises new minority points by interpolating between fraud neighbours, inside an imblearn pipeline Gives the learner many more minority examples Synthetic points may not resemble real fraud; can create noise in overlapping regions; larger training set
C. scale_pos_weight (XGBoost) Gradient-boosting equivalent of class weighting Native, efficient, no resampling Changes probability calibration; needs a threshold review

SMOTE lives inside the pipeline, so during cross-validation it is re-fitted on each training fold only, and it is never applied to validation or test data.

The 5-fold cross-validation on the training set (SMOTE re-fitted inside each fold) confirms the logistic-regression pattern: class weighting and in-fold SMOTE give almost identical PR-AUC (0.737 ± 0.053 vs 0.735 ± 0.052) and recall (0.905 vs 0.897).

Key insight. In this dataset, weighting and SMOTE mainly move the operating point: they push probabilities upwards so that more transactions cross 0.5. They do not improve the model's underlying ability to rank fraud above legitimate transactions (PR-AUC is flat or slightly lower). The same recall/precision trade-off can be reached more transparently by tuning the decision threshold, which is done in Stage 16. The large jump in PR-AUC comes from changing the algorithm (LR → XGBoost), not from resampling.

Stage 15 — Model Building & Comparison¶

Decision Tree and Random Forest are added (with class weighting, the cheapest effective strategy for these learners). Hyperparameters are sensible defaults with light regularisation; no extensive tuning was performed (see Future Improvements).

Selection rule (fixed before looking at results): the primary criterion is validation PR-AUC, because it summarises precision–recall performance across all thresholds and is not inflated by the huge number of true negatives. The operating threshold is chosen afterwards in Stage 16, so default-threshold precision/recall are reported but are not the selection criterion. Accuracy is shown only to illustrate why it is not used.

    axes[1].plot(fpr, tpr, lw=lw, label=f"{name} (AUC={roc_auc_score(y_val, p):.3f})")
axes[0].axhline(y_val.mean(), ls="--", c="grey", label="random (prevalence)")
axes[0].set_xlabel("Recall"); axes[0].set_ylabel("Precision"); axes[0].set_title("Validation precision-recall curves")
axes[1].plot([0, 1], [0, 1], "--", c="grey"); axes[1].set_xscale("log"); axes[1].set_xlim(1e-5, 1)
axes[1].set_xlabel("False positive rate (log)"); axes[1].set_ylabel("True positive rate"); axes[1].set_title("Validation ROC curves")
axes[0].legend(fontsize=7); axes[1].legend(fontsize=7)
save_fig("s15_model_curves")

Model comparison (validation set, sorted by PR-AUC). XGBoost without weighting has the highest PR-AUC (0.886), followed closely by XGBoost with scale_pos_weight (0.884), Random Forest (0.871) and XGBoost + SMOTE (0.867). All logistic-regression variants sit around 0.79–0.80, and the shallow Decision Tree is weakest (0.695, with 487 false positives at the default threshold). The accuracy column ranges only from 0.970 to 0.9997 and would have been an uninformative selection criterion.

Selected model: XGBoost (no weighting). It was chosen by the pre-specified rule (highest validation PR-AUC). It also offers the best precision at the default threshold (0.975), which keeps analyst workload low, and it trains in about 7 seconds compared with about 130 seconds for Random Forest.

Honest caveat: the gap to XGBoost + scale_pos_weight (0.002 PR-AUC) is well within the noise expected from 94 validation frauds. The two XGBoost variants are effectively tied in ranking quality and differ mainly in where the 0.5 threshold falls, which the threshold analysis below addresses directly.

Stage 16 — Model Evaluation, Threshold Analysis & Explainability¶

16.1 Choosing the operating threshold on the validation set¶

The default 0.5 cut-off is arbitrary. Because missing fraud is typically costlier than reviewing a false alarm, but no cost figures are available in this dataset, the threshold is chosen to maximise F2 on the validation set (F2 weights recall twice as heavily as precision). The F1-optimal threshold is shown for comparison. The test set is not used for this choice.

In [54]:
best_model = MODELS[BEST_NAME]["model"]
val_p = MODELS[BEST_NAME]["val_proba"]

grid_thr = np.round(np.arange(0.01, 1.00, 0.01), 2)
sweep = pd.DataFrame([evaluate(BEST_NAME, y_val, val_p, t) for t in grid_thr]).set_index("Threshold")
sweep["F2"] = [fbeta_score(y_val, (val_p >= t).astype(int), beta=2, zero_division=0) for t in grid_thr]
THR_F2 = float(sweep["F2"].idxmax()); THR_F1 = float(sweep["F1"].idxmax())
print(f"F2-optimal threshold on validation: {THR_F2:.2f}  |  F1-optimal threshold: {THR_F1:.2f}")
display(sweep.loc[sorted({0.05, 0.1, 0.2, THR_F2, THR_F1, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9}), ["Precision", "Recall", "F1", "F2", "TP", "FP", "FN"]])

How stable are these test numbers? The test set contains fewer than 100 frauds, so each missed fraud moves recall by roughly one percentage point. A bootstrap (1,000 resamples of the test set, model and threshold fixed) gives a 95% interval for the headline metrics.

Threshold selection (validation). Both the F2-optimal and the F1-optimal threshold on the validation set is 0.43: precision 0.964, recall 0.851 (80 of 94 caught, 3 false positives, 14 missed). Lowering the threshold to 0.05 on validation would catch only 2 more frauds while adding 12 more false positives.

Final test results (untouched set, 56,746 transactions, 95 frauds) at threshold 0.43:

  • Precision 0.9865, recall 0.7684, F1 0.8639, ROC-AUC 0.9731, PR-AUC 0.8332
  • Confusion matrix: 73 frauds caught (TP), 1 false alarm (FP), 22 frauds missed (FN), 56,650 correctly approved (TN)
  • On the test set, threshold 0.43 gives the same predictions as 0.50, because no test transaction scores between 0.30 and 0.50.
  • The baseline logistic regression on the same test set achieves PR-AUC 0.698 and recall 0.589 (56 caught, 39 missed, 9 false alarms), so the selected model catches 17 more frauds with 8 fewer false alarms.
  • Bootstrap 95% intervals: PR-AUC 0.757–0.903, recall 0.684–0.846, precision 0.956–1.000. Validation recall (0.851) sits at the top of the test interval. The difference corresponds to a handful of frauds and is consistent with small-sample variation, but it signals that ≈ 0.77–0.85 recall is a realistic expectation rather than a guarantee.

The business trade-off (test set).

Threshold Alerts Frauds caught False alarms Frauds missed Recall Precision % of fraud value caught
0.05 96 76 20 19 0.800 0.792 74.4%
0.10 83 75 8 20 0.789 0.904 74.3%
0.20 76 73 3 22 0.768 0.961 74.3%
0.43 (selected) 74 73 1 22 0.768 0.987 74.3%
0.70 68 67 1 28 0.705 0.985 60.2%
0.90 64 63 1 32 0.663 0.984 49.3%
  • Raising the threshold above 0.43 buys almost nothing in precision (it is already 0.987) but loses frauds quickly: at 0.90, 10 more frauds are missed and the share of fraud value caught falls from 74.3% to 49.3%.
  • Lowering the threshold to 0.05 catches only 3 more frauds (recall 0.768 → 0.800) at the cost of 19 extra false alarms, and those 3 frauds are low-value (fraud value caught rises by only 7.55).
  • The model's scores are strongly polarised. Most of the 22 missed frauds (3,792.56 of value, 25.7% of test fraud value) receive scores so low that no reasonable threshold would catch them without flooding the queue. This is consistent with M3/M8, where a minority of frauds look statistically like legitimate transactions. Recovering them will require new information (features), not threshold tuning.

What drives the model's predictions.

  • Permutation importance (drop in validation PR-AUC when a feature is shuffled): V14 (0.046) ≫ V4 (0.033) > V10 (0.022) > Amount (0.010) > V12 (0.006). The remaining features each contribute less than 0.006.
  • SHAP (mean |SHAP| on a validation sample with all 94 frauds): V14 (1.81) and V4 (1.35) dominate, followed by V12 (0.61), V8, V3, V11, V15, V10, V17 and Amount (10th, 0.24). The SHAP summary plot shows the direction: low V14 values push predictions towards fraud and high V4 values push towards fraud. This matches the class-conditional analysis in B7 and B9.
  • The model-native (gain) ranking and the two model-agnostic methods agree on the core features (V14, V4, V10/V12). These are also the top KS-ranked variables found independently in EDA, which is a reassuring consistency check.
  • V8 ranks 4th by SHAP despite being only 18th by KS separation. A plausible reading is that it adds information conditional on the main components (an interaction), which univariate analysis cannot reveal.

Interpretation limits. V1–V28 are anonymised PCA components, so "low V14 increases fraud risk" is a statement about a statistical direction, not about any identifiable customer or merchant behaviour. Importance measures show what the model relies on, not what causes fraud. Because Amount is correlated with V2/V5/V7 (M1), its importance may be partly shared with those components.

Executive Summary¶

This project analysed 283,726 credit-card transactions (after removing 1,081 exact duplicates) recorded over 48 hours, of which 473 (0.1667%) were fraudulent. The aim was to give the Fraud Risk Manager a model that ranks transactions by fraud risk and an evidence-based view of the precision/recall trade-off. The approach was: a full data-quality review; 10 KPIs and 30 univariate, bivariate and multivariate analyses; a leakage-free 60/20/20 stratified split; a logistic-regression baseline; a comparison of class weighting, SMOTE (training folds only) and scale_pos_weight; four model families; selection on validation PR-AUC; threshold choice on validation; and a single final evaluation on the untouched test set, with bootstrap intervals and SHAP/permutation explainability.

Key Findings¶

  1. Accuracy is meaningless here. "Approve everything" scores 99.83% accuracy and catches no fraud.
  2. Fraud matters more in value than in count. Fraud is 0.1667% of transactions but 0.2334% of value. The average fraud (123.87) exceeds the average genuine transaction (88.41), although the median fraud (9.82) is smaller than the median genuine transaction (22.00).
  3. Amount risk is U-shaped. Zero-value transactions have 8.3× the average fraud rate and 0–1 transactions 3.1×, while 500–1,000 has 2.4× and 10–50 is the safest band (0.37×).
  4. Quiet periods are riskier. Elapsed hours 1–6 carry 7.15% of volume but 24.95% of fraud (with the caveat of only two days of data).
  5. A few anonymised components carry most of the signal. V14, V10, V12, V4, V11 and V17 separate the classes far better than Amount or Time (KS 0.74–0.84 vs 0.27 for Amount and 0.16 for Time). The lowest V14 decile holds 90.1% of fraud.
  6. Fraud has a coordinated multivariate signature. Within fraud, the top components are strongly inter-correlated (mean |r| 0.74 vs 0.09 for legitimate). Transactions with 4 or more simultaneous extreme signals are 64–88% fraud.
  7. About 12.5% of frauds look ordinary on every top component. These are the frauds that every model struggles to catch.
  8. Resampling and weighting shifted the operating point but did not improve ranking. PR-AUC was flat for LR (0.79–0.80) and not better for XGBoost. Changing the algorithm to gradient boosting raised validation PR-AUC from 0.798 to 0.886.

Business Recommendations¶

  1. Use the model as a risk score, not a yes/no flag. Its scores are strongly polarised, so a high-score band (≥ 0.43) can be actioned with high confidence: on test, 73 of 74 alerts were real fraud.
  2. Add a tiered response. Send scores ≥ 0.43 to block or high-priority review. Send a lower band (≈ 0.05–0.43) to step-up authentication rather than outright decline. On test this band contained 3 frauds and 19 genuine transactions, a friction cost that a light-touch challenge can absorb.
  3. Prioritise human investigation by value. High-value transactions with a fraud-like V14 profile showed a 22.3% fraud rate (M6). Review queues should be ordered by score × amount.
  4. Monitor the threshold, don't fix it forever. Precision and recall moved materially between 0.43 and 0.90 (recall 0.77 → 0.66, fraud value caught 74% → 49%). Track alert volume, precision and recall weekly and revisit the threshold when fraud patterns or review capacity change.
  5. Pay specific attention to zero/micro-value and quiet-period transactions as candidate rule-based or monitoring segments, after confirming the pattern on longer history.
  6. Invest in data for the "hidden" fraud. About a quarter of test fraud value was missed at any reasonable threshold. These cases need new information (see Future Improvements), not a lower cut-off.

Limitations¶

  • Severe class imbalance: only 473 frauds in total and fewer than 100 in each of the validation and test sets, so metrics carry wide confidence intervals.
  • Anonymised PCA variables: V1–V28 cannot be translated into business rules or customer-facing explanations.
  • Limited business context: no merchant, channel, geography, device or cost information, so false-positive and false-negative costs could not be quantified, and thresholds were chosen with F2 as a proxy.
  • Historical, short observation period: 48 hours from a past period, so weekly and seasonal patterns and the true clock time are unknown.
  • No cardholder identifiers: customer-level behaviour (velocity, deviation from personal norms) cannot be modelled.
  • Concept drift: fraud tactics change, and performance on this snapshot will decay.
  • No causal inference: all findings are associations.
  • Random (not temporal) split: this may be optimistic relative to real forward-in-time deployment.

Future Improvements¶

  • Additional features: cardholder history, velocity counts, merchant category, device, geolocation and channel.
  • Cost-sensitive modelling: optimise expected loss using real fraud-loss and review-cost figures instead of F2.
  • Probability calibration: Platt or isotonic scaling, so scores can be read as probabilities for loss forecasting.
  • Temporal validation: train on past data, test on later periods, once a longer history is available.
  • Hyperparameter optimisation: for example, Bayesian search with stratified CV on PR-AUC.
  • Anomaly detection: for example, Isolation Forest or autoencoders as a complementary signal for novel fraud.
  • Production monitoring: score-distribution and feature drift (PSI), alert precision, and recall from chargeback feedback.
  • Retraining policy: scheduled plus drift-triggered retraining, with champion/challenger comparison.
  • Deployment: a real-time scoring API with latency SLAs, an audit log and human-in-the-loop review tooling.
